pages.summary: The gamma function, and its logarithm.
body: `gamma(x)` is the integral from 0 to infinity of `t^(x-1)*exp(-t)`; for whole numbers `gamma(n+1)` is `n!`, and it fills in the values between them. It has poles at 0 and the negative whole numbers, and overflows above about 171; `gammaln` gives `log(gamma(x))` for positive `x` without overflowing, for ratios of large factorials.
syntax: The gamma function of each element.

examples.title: The curve and its poles

pages.summary: The regularized incomplete gamma function, and its inverse.
body: `gammainc(x, a)` is the integral of `t^(a-1)*exp(-t)` from 0 to `x`, divided by `gamma(a)`: the cumulative distribution function of the gamma distribution with shape `a`, rising from 0 to 1. `'upper'` gives `1 - gammainc(x, a)` accurately in the tail; the scaled forms multiply by `gamma(a+1)*exp(x)/x^a`. Note the order: `x` first, then `a`. `gammaincinv(y, a)` gives the `x` with `gammainc(x, a) = y`.

examples.title: Curves for three shapes
A Poisson probability, and a median
examples.intro: The probability of at most 3 events when 2 are expected is the upper function at x = 2, a = 4.

pages.summary: The beta function, and its logarithm.
body: `beta(z, w)` is the integral from 0 to 1 of `t^(z-1)*(1-t)^(w-1)`, equal to `gamma(z)*gamma(w)/gamma(z+w)`. For large arguments it underflows to 0; `betaln` gives its logarithm.

examples.title: The function and its relation to gamma

pages.summary: The regularized incomplete beta function, and its inverse.
body: `betainc(x, z, w)` is the integral of `t^(z-1)*(1-t)^(w-1)` from 0 to `x`, divided by `beta(z, w)`: the cumulative distribution function of the beta distribution. `'upper'` gives `1 - betainc(x, z, w)` accurately; `betaincinv(y, z, w)` gives the `x` with `betainc(x, z, w) = y`.

examples.title: A binomial tail, and a median
examples.intro: The chance of at least 7 successes in 10 trials with p = 0.5 is betainc(0.5, 7, 4).

examples.title: Curves for three shapes

pages.summary: The error function, its complement, and the scaled complement.
body: `erf(x)` is `2/sqrt(pi)` times the integral of `exp(-t^2)` from 0 to `x`: the chance that a normal value lies within `x*sqrt(2)` standard deviations of the mean. `erfc(x)` is `1 - erf(x)`, computed so that it stays accurate where `erf(x)` is nearly 1; `erfcx(x)` is `exp(x^2)*erfc(x)`, which neither overflows nor underflows for large `x`.

examples.title: Within one, two and three standard deviations
The curves

pages.summary: The inverse error function, and the inverse complementary error function.
body: `erfinv(y)` gives the `x` with `erf(x) = y` for y in [-1, 1]; `erfcinv(y)` the `x` with `erfc(x) = y` for y in [0, 2], accurate when `y` is tiny, where `1 - y` would round to 1. Times `sqrt(2)`, they give normal quantiles.

The integral of `exp(-t)/t` from `x` to infinity: large near 0 and falling off like `exp(-x)/x`. Negative and complex arguments give the analytic continuation, complex on the negative axis. In groundwater hydraulics it is the well function of the Theis solution.

examples.title: Drawdown around a pumped well (Theis)
examples.intro: s = Q/(4πT)·E1(r²S/(4Tt)), here 10 m from a well pumped at 10 L/s, transmissivity 1e-3 m²/s, storativity 1e-4.

pages.summary: The digamma function (the derivative of gammaln), or its higher derivatives.
body: `psi(x)` is `gamma'(x)/gamma(x)`; `psi(k, x)` is its k-th derivative (the trigamma function for k = 1). At whole numbers, `psi(n+1)` is the harmonic number `1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n` minus Euler's constant.

examples.title: Euler's constant, a harmonic number, and pi^2/6

pages.summary: Bessel functions of the first and second kind, J and Y.
body: The solutions of Bessel's equation `x^2*y'' + x*y' + (x^2 - nu^2)*y = 0`, which appear in waves and diffusion in circles and cylinders. `J` is finite at 0; `Y` goes to minus infinity there. Both oscillate and decay like `1/sqrt(x)`. The order `nu` need not be whole, and a row of orders with a column of points gives a table; with 1 as the third input, the result is scaled by `exp(-abs(imag(z)))`.

examples.title: J0, J1 and J2
Y0 and Y1
The first zero of J0, where a drumhead's lowest mode has its rim

pages.summary: Modified Bessel functions of the first and second kind, I and K.
body: The solutions of `x^2*y'' + x*y' - (x^2 + nu^2)*y = 0`: `I` grows like `exp(x)/sqrt(x)` and `K` decays like `exp(-x)/sqrt(x)`, as in heat conduction and diffusion around cylinders. With 1 as the third input they are scaled, `I` by `exp(-abs(real(z)))` and `K` by `exp(z)`, to stay finite far out.

examples.title: The two kinds
Scaled where the plain one overflows

pages.summary: The Hankel functions, Bessel functions of the third kind.
body: `H1 = J + iY` and `H2 = J - iY`, waves travelling outward and inward from a cylinder. `besselh(nu, z)` is the first kind; `besselh(nu, k, z)` takes the kind `k` (1 or 2).

pages.summary: The Airy functions Ai and Bi, and their derivatives.
body: The solutions of `y'' = x*y`: oscillating for negative `x`, and for positive `x` decaying (`Ai`) or growing (`Bi`). They describe light near a caustic and a quantum particle in a uniform field. `k` selects 0 for Ai, 1 for Ai', 2 for Bi and 3 for Bi'; with 1 as the third input the results are scaled.

examples.title: Ai and Bi

pages.summary: Complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kind, K(m) and E(m).
body: `K(m)` is the integral from 0 to `pi/2` of `1/sqrt(1 - m*sin(t)^2)` and `E(m)` of `sqrt(1 - m*sin(t)^2)`, for the parameter m in [0, 1]. They give a pendulum's period at any amplitude and the perimeter of an ellipse.

examples.title: A pendulum's period, against the small-swing period
examples.intro: A pendulum swinging out to θ0 takes 2K(m)/π times the small-swing period, with m = sin²(θ0/2).

examples.title: The perimeter of an ellipse
examples.intro: With semi-axes a and b, the perimeter is 4a·E(1 - b²/a²).

pages.summary: The Jacobi elliptic functions sn, cn and dn.
body: For the parameter m in [0, 1]: `sn(u)` and `cn(u)` are the sine and cosine of the amplitude `phi` where the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind reaches `u`, and `dn = sqrt(1 - m*sn^2)`. With m = 0 they are `sin`, `cos` and 1; they have period `4K(m)`, and describe the swing of a pendulum at large amplitude.

examples.title: One period at m = 0.9

pages.summary: Associated Legendre functions of degree n, for each order m from 0 to n.
body: A row for each order m = 0, 1, ..., n and a column for each `x` in [-1, 1]: `P(1, :)` is the Legendre polynomial of degree n. `'sch'` gives the Schmidt semi-normalized functions, used for geomagnetic fields, and `'norm'` the fully normalized ones.

examples.title: The Legendre polynomials P0 to P4
examples.code:
x = linspace(-1, 1, 200);
hold on
for n = 0:4
    P = legendre(n, x);
    plot(x, P(1, :))
end
hold off, grid on, ylim([-1 1.2])
legend('P_0', 'P_1', 'P_2', 'P_3', 'P_4', 'Location', 'south')

body: `sinint(x)` is the integral from 0 to `x` of `sin(t)/t`, tending to `pi/2`; `cosint(x)` is Euler's constant plus `log(x)` plus the integral from 0 to `x` of `(cos(t) - 1)/t`, tending to 0, and complex for negative `x`. Symbolic input gives the symbolic functions.

examples.title: The curves
The overshoot of a square wave's Fourier series
examples.intro: Near a jump, the partial sums overshoot to 2/π·Si(π) times the step, however many terms are summed.

body: `exp(-x^2)` times the integral from 0 to `x` of `exp(t^2)`. It rises to a maximum of about 0.541 near x = 0.924 and then falls like `1/(2x)`; it appears in the line shapes of spectroscopy and in plasma physics.

examples.title: The curve and its maximum

pages.summary: The Fresnel sine and cosine integrals.
body: `fresnels(x)` is the integral from 0 to `x` of `sin(pi*t^2/2)` and `fresnelc(x)` of `cos(pi*t^2/2)`; both tend to 1/2. Drawn against each other they make the Euler (Cornu) spiral, a curve whose curvature grows in step with its length, used for road and railway transitions and in diffraction at an edge.

examples.title: The Euler spiral
examples.code:
t = linspace(-5, 5, 1000);
plot(fresnelc(t), fresnels(t)), axis equal, grid on

examples.title: Slowly toward one half
examples.intro: Far out they oscillate within about 1/(πx) of 1/2.
